name: Alvaro Hernández
description:
Alvaro Luna Hernandez was a political organizer with Cesar Chavez and the Chicano Movement who in 1975, was charged with the murder of a motel clerk after a former employee told police they witnessed Hernandez kill him in a robbery. No money was actually taken from the motel and no other evidence connected Hernandez to the crime. The witness was granted full immunity for a number of unrelated offenses in exchange for her testimony and she later recanted and claimed and she was instructed to testify that Hernandez committed the murder under threat of prosecution. While in jail, Hernandez became a jailhouse lawyer and helped other inmates who had been falsely convicted appeal their sentences including death row inmate Aldape Guerra whose conviction was overturned after Hernandez gathered the evidence to show he was framed for killing a police officer.

In 1991, Hernandez was released after serving 16 years. Hernandez spent the next 5 years organizing politically until in 1996 the local Sheriff ordered a deputy to go to Hernadez's home and arrest him for a convenience store robbery based only on the fact the robber was described as being Hispanic. Police knew he hadn't committed the robbery as Hernandez was under police surveillance for activism at the time and undercover cops were watching him on the other side of town during the time of the robbery. Police also went against normal protocol by sending only a single deputy to arrest what they claimed was an armed criminal. Hernandez asserts that the deputy put a gun to head and made it clear he was about to kill him and he responded by knocking the gun from the cop's hand and fleeing the scene before later surrendering to police. Hernandez was convicted of assaulting the police officer by knocking the gun from his hand and given the maximum sentence of 50 years.

Chicano political prisoner, prolific jailhouse lawyer, and longtime member of the Movimiento de Liberacion Nacional Mexicano. His earlier life sentence arose from a murder prosecution in Pecos County, Texas; that imprisonment ended in 1991. His current sentence is 50 years for aggravated assault of a peace officer. According to documents obtained after trial, the state used perjured testimony and suppressed crime-lab reports and other favorable evidence that would have cleared him; he has consistently maintained his innocence. While incarcerated he became a leading prison-reform litigator in Texas, contributing to the landmark Ruiz v. Estelle systemwide class action and to a civil-rights suit charging the Texas Governor and Parole Board with racial discrimination against Chicano and Black prisoners. Spent eight consecutive years in solitary confinement in retaliation for his organizing — a 1984 prison report justified the isolation by quoting his "own statements concerning political beliefs." Held at Goree Unit and elsewhere in the Texas Department of Criminal Justice. During that earlier imprisonment, he became eligible for parole in 1986 but was repeatedly denied before his 1991 release.

name: Antonio Guerrero
description:
Antonio Guerrero Rodriguez is part of the Cuban Five, serving a sentence of life imprisonment plus 10 years, and is in U.S.P. Florence, Colorado. He was convicted of espionage, conspiracy to commit murder, and other illegal activities in the United States after monitoring Cuban-exile terrorist groups.

Biography

Antonio Guerrero Rodriguez was born in the city of Miami on October 16, 1958. His parents were both from Cuba and immediately after the initiation of the Cuban Revolution in 1959, they returned to Cuba. In 1983, Guerrero graduated as Airfield Construction Engineer in Kiev, Ukraine. The expansion of the Santiago de Cuba International Airport was the most important work in which he was involved. Guerrero is a poet and has penned a considerable number of poems, a selection of which has been published in English and Spanish under the title "Desde Mi Altura" (From My Altitude). Guerrero has become an accomplished artist and his art and poetry can be viewed on his website. He has two sons, 20 year old, Antonio, and 15 year old, Gabriel.

Case

Fore more than 40 years, anti-Cuba terrorist organizations based in Miami have engaged in countless terrorist activities against Cuba, and against anyone who advocates a normalization of relations between the US and Cuba. More than 3,000 Cubans have died as a result of these terrorists' attacks.

Terrorist Miami groups like Commandos F4 and Brothers to the Rescue operate with complete

impunity from within the United States to attack Cuba -- with the knowledge and support of the FBI and CIA.

Therefore, Cuba made the careful and necessary decision to send the Five Cubans to Miami to monitor the terrorists. The Cuban Five infiltrated the terrorist organizations in Miami to inform Cuba of imminent attacks.

The aim of such a clandestine operation by the Cuban Five -- at great personal risk -- was to prevent criminal acts, and thus protect the lives of Cubans and other people.

But, instead of arresting the terrorists, the FBI arrested the Cuban Five, ANTI-TERRORISTS, on September 12, 1998. The Five were illegally held in solitary confinement for 17 months in a Miami Jail.

The trail began in November 2000. With the seven-month trail based in Miami, a virtual witchhunt atmosphere existed. Defense attorneys' motions for a change of venue was denied five times by the judge, although it was obvious that a fair trail was impossible in that city.

In a blow to justice, the Cuban Five were convicted June 8, 2001 and sentenced to four life terms and 75 years in December, 2001.

name: Bradford Lyttle
description: Bradford Lyttle is an American pacifist organizer whose arrests span more than half a century, from draft refusal in the early 1950s to a nuclear weapons plant in 2010. He first went to prison in 1954, serving nine months at the United States Medical Center for Federal Prisoners in Springfield, Missouri for refusing to cooperate with Selective Service. In 1959 he organized Omaha Action, the nonviolent campaign against the intercontinental ballistic missile base at Mead, Nebraska; arrested on July 8 and bailed, he was sentenced on July 13 to six months and a $500 fine for trespassing and disregarding a court order. He coordinated the Quebec-to-Guantanamo peace walk of 1963 and 1964, which carried the pacifist movement into the segregated South and was jailed repeatedly along the way — at Macon, Georgia in November 1963, and twice at Albany, Georgia, where the walkers insisted on marching integrated through the downtown business district and spent the turn of 1964 in jail. He was arrested at the Times Square antiwar sit-down in February 1966, and that April he and five other American pacifists were seized in Saigon while trying to demonstrate near the United States Embassy and deported to Hong Kong within hours. Arrests followed at the Pentagon in 1967 and in the Mayday actions of 1971. He remained active for decades afterwards, arrested with David Dellinger at the 1996 Democratic National Convention protest in Chicago, acquitted by directed verdict after a 2005 Chicago demonstration against the Iraq war when the court found police had not allowed adequate time to disperse, and arrested again at the Y-12 nuclear weapons complex in Oak Ridge, Tennessee in July 2010, at the age of eighty-two. He was born on November 20, 1927.

description:
Daniel Sicken is described as an anti-nuclear activist whose direct action centered on U.S. intercontinental ballistic missile infrastructure. In August 1998, he and a co-defendant entered a missile-site area in Colorado as a symbolic act of “disarmament,” using tools and blood imagery to protest the existence and planned use of nuclear weapons. They remained on site and were arrested, treating detention as an expected outcome of the action.

Federal prosecutors pursued serious felony charges that framed the protest as sabotage and destruction of government property. Sicken was convicted and sentenced to a multi-year federal prison term, with the case later discussed in legal and policy debates about how broadly “sabotage” statutes can be applied to nonviolent protest actions at military facilities. On August 6, 1998 (Hiroshima Day) Daniel Sicken and Oliver Sachio Coe entered Minuteman III nuclear missile silo "N-9" near Concrete, North Dakota, and hammered on its silo lid as the "Minuteman III Plowshares" disarmament action. They were prosecuted in federal court (D. North Dakota).

Pennsylvania police working a patrol detail at a swap meet discovered Cummings purchasing pyrite crystals which radio hobbyists use to build armature radio receivers. Despite these crystals not being illegal to buy or sell, police confiscated them claiming they could be drugs along with more of Cummings property, including novelty cold war era spy books he owned that police claimed to be suspicious. After the United States Secret Service inquired about the seized property they informed local police that some of the items could be used for, "illicit purposes." Cummings was then charged with being in possession of a Radio Shack Tone Dialer and Thinkpad Laptop which violated a vague law that prohibited owning objects that could be used for unauthorized telecommunications access. This law effectively made owning a computer a crime regardless of if the computer was used for criminal activity. He pled guilty to this charge and was sent to prison. While awaiting a parole hearing, he was charged by Bucks County, Pennsylvania prison officials with misuse of the telephone system for receiving a call from a reporter who wanted to interview him regarding his case. Cummings was then moved to a high-security facility, where he was brutally beaten by a fellow inmate who broke Cummings jaw and arm.

On August 18th 1991 Thompson called police for the second time to request they provide her protection out fear her ex-boyfriend was planning to kill her. Thompson retrieved a handgun she had bought for self defense when she discovered him in the home and shot her ex-partner as he lunged at her. She then immediately called 911 to report the shooting. Thompson was initially told the case was clear self-defense and she wouldn't be charged but District Attorney John Thompson insisted on indicting her for first degree murder. name: Fred Hampton Jr.
description: Fred Hampton Jr. is an activist in the Uhuru Movement and the son of famed Black Panther leader Fred Hampton. In 1989, Hampton was charged with two counts of murder and armed robbery. After numerous alibis proved Hampton was at a local park when the crime was supposed to have taken place the charges were dropped. The prosecutor reportedly shouted in the court room that they would, "Get Fred next time" after the Judge ordered the charges dismissed. In 1992 Hampton Jr. was again arrested for arson after someone threw Molotov Cocktails at a Korean business during the L.A Riots. The Molotov Cocktails thrown in the attempted arson failed to ignite and caused little damage. A local gang member named Warren Gilbert told police, "the guy who sells the Burning Spear Newspaper probably did it." and claimed to have recognized Hampton running from the crime scene and nearly being hit by a bus during his escape. Fred Hampton Jr. alleges his only interaction with Gilbert had been months before his arrest he was threatened by Gilbert whom he had never met before after he approached him outside of a movie theater. During the trial Hampton provided an alibi for the day or the arson. No physical evidence linked Hampton to the Molotov Cocktails and fingerprints found on them did not match Hamptons. Prosecutors found no other witnesses besides Gilbert and could not produce the driver of the bus who Gilbert claimed to have seen nearly strike Hampton as he ran from the crime scene. During the trial prosecutors alleged that the Uhuru Movement was a gang and Fred Hampton Jr. was a gang leader and cited an article he had written in the Burning Spear Newspaper where he criticizes neo-colonial business practices as the motivation for the attack. Hampton was found guilty and sentenced to 18 years in prison.

name: Jennifer Rose
description:
Jennifer Amelia Rose — formerly known as Jennifer Gann, and called "Babygirl" by supporters — is a transgender woman, jailhouse lawyer, writer, and prison abolitionist who has been incarcerated in California since 1990. Of white and Cherokee heritage, she has become a widely supported voice against the abuse of LGBTQ and gender-nonconforming people behind bars.

Originally sentenced to seven years for armed robbery, Rose became a militant jailhouse lawyer and organizer, taking part in prison protests and direct action through the early 1990s. After being beaten by guards at Folsom Prison, she fought back; the resulting charges — including weapons possession and assault on a district attorney and an associate warden — brought multiple sentences of 25 years to life under California's "Three Strikes" law in 1995–1996, turning a fixed term into what amounts to a life sentence.

She survived more than a decade in solitary confinement, including the Security Housing Units at Pelican Bay State Prison (1994–2004) and Tehachapi (2010–2011) — conditions widely condemned as torture.

Rose came out as a bisexual trans woman in 2006. She has organized alongside anarchist, feminist, and queer prison abolitionists and the Maoist MIM (Prisons), served for five years in the leadership of Black & Pink, and is a prolific writer, blogger, poet, and artist whose work documents the realities faced by trans prisoners.

In 2018 she won a California Supreme Court ruling granting reconsideration of her sentence, and she has continued to pursue relief, including resentencing under Proposition 36, the Three Strikes Reform Act. She remains imprisoned at Salinas Valley State Prison in Soledad, California.

description:
John Dear is an American peace activist, Catholic priest (formerly a Jesuit; he was dismissed from the Society of Jesus in 2014 over his political activism, and has continued his ministry as a diocesan priest), author, and lecturer. He has been arrested approximately 80 times for civil-disobedience actions against war, nuclear weapons, the U.S. School of the Americas, and U.S. drone warfare since the 1980s.

His most significant federal sentence came after the December 7, 1993 Pax Christi-USA Plowshares action at Seymour Johnson Air Force Base in Goldsboro, North Carolina. name: Keith LaMar
description:
Keith LaMar, who has taken the name Bomani Shakur in prison, is an Ohio death row prisoner whose case is among the most contested wrongful-conviction cases in U.S. capital litigation. He was 19 years old and serving an 18-year sentence for an unrelated 1989 manslaughter when, on April 11, 1993, the Lucasville Prison Uprising began at the Southern Ohio Correctional Facility. Over the eleven days of the uprising one prison guard and nine prisoners were killed. LaMar was charged with five of the prisoner killings and tried by an all-white jury in 1995 in rural Lawrence County, Ohio. He was sentenced to death.

He has consistently maintained his innocence. The state has never produced any physical evidence connecting him to the killings; the conviction rested entirely on the testimony of incarcerated witnesses, several of whom received reductions in their own sentences in exchange. Years of post-conviction litigation have established that the prosecution failed to disclose statements from other prisoners identifying different killers — Brady violations the federal courts have nonetheless declined to remedy.

He has spent the past three decades in solitary confinement, almost entirely at the Ohio State Penitentiary supermax in Youngstown. His memoir Condemned: The Whole Story (2014) is widely cited in U.S. carceral writing. His scheduled execution date of January 13, 2027 (rescheduled from 2023 by Governor DeWine) makes him one of the most prominent imprisoned writers in the United States.

name: Keith McHenry
description:
Keith McHenry is an American activist and co-founder of Food Not Bombs, a global all-volunteer movement that recovers surplus food and shares free vegan and vegetarian meals in public spaces as a protest against war, poverty, and the destruction of the environment.

Born in Frankfurt, West Germany in 1957 while his father was stationed there with the U.S. Army, McHenry grew up moving between U.S. National Parks where his father later worked as a park ranger, including Yosemite, Grand Canyon, Big Bend, Shenandoah, and the Everglades. He began studying painting and sculpture at Boston University in 1975, where he also took a course in American history with Howard Zinn. While in Boston he became active with the Clamshell Alliance, traveling repeatedly to Seabrook, New Hampshire to protest nuclear power. In 1980 he and seven friends co-founded the first Food Not Bombs chapter in Cambridge, Massachusetts, distributing uncooked food to housing projects and shelters and serving vegetarian meals in Harvard Square and on Boston Common.

After moving to San Francisco in 1988, McHenry started a second Food Not Bombs group. On August 15, 1988 he was among nine volunteers arrested in Golden Gate Park for sharing food and literature without a permit. Over the following years he was arrested more than 100 times for serving free food in city parks and spent over 500 nights in jail. Under California's Three Strikes Law he faced a sentence of 25 years to life. In 1995, after a sustained international campaign by Amnesty International and the United Nations Human Rights Commission — which classified him as a prisoner of conscience — the charges were ultimately dropped.

McHenry also co-founded Homes Not Jails, a group that helps homeless people occupy abandoned buildings, and contributed to the founding of the Independent Media Center. In 2005 he coordinated Food Not Bombs' food, clothing, and supply relief for survivors of Hurricane Katrina. He has received the San Francisco Bay Guardian's 1999 Local Hero Award, the War Resisters League's Resister of the Year award in 1995, and the Justice Studies Association's 2012 Noam Chomsky Award.

Food Not Bombs has grown to hundreds of autonomous chapters across the United States, Canada, Europe, Latin America, Asia, Africa, and Australia.

description: Lise Olsen was a nurse and animal rights activist who on July 4, 1992 hung a banner in protest of fur farms over a railroad bridge near her home. The banner was illuminated by homemade lanterns. The FBI claimed the lanterns which were made of peanut butter jars were explosive devices despite bomb experts stating they had no incendiary or explosive capacity. During the trial the judge allows prosecutors to refer to Olsen as a terrorist in front of the jury and police officers without expertise falsely testify the lanterns were weapons. Olsen was convicted and sentenced to 4 years in prison despite the trial judge promising probation. While in prison the FBI attempted to charge Olsen with an incident where a consumer grade smoke grenade used in paintball games was found inside the fur section of a local department store. The smoke grenade was not ignited and fingerprints found on them did not match Olsen. No evidence connected Olsen to the grenades and the FBI falsely claimed the smoke grenade was a bomb. Prosecutors attempted multiple times to bring charges against her related to this incident but the Grand Jury refused to indict. The FBI then claimed to be investigating a murder they said Olsen was involved with despite no murder having occurred as pretext to detain family and friends of Olsen for interviews and fingerprinting. During her parole hearing, those who spoke on her behalf including an elderly civil rights activist were soon questioned by the FBI about their connection to her and fingerprinted. On August 4, 1995 her conviction was overturned and a new trial was ordered after a detective admitted during a deposition that he had lied when he claimed Olsen had told him she manufactured Molotov Cocktails. During the new trial Olsen was acquitted of all felonies involving incendiary devices and attempted arson but convicted on, "Unauthorized Use of a Weapon" for possessing more than three tablespoons of gasoline fuel after the jury was falsely instructed on the meaning of the statute and only told it requires someone possess something that could be used as a weapon rather than requiring they intend to use it as a weapon. Mark Peter Colville, age 56, KBP7 defendant; 18 months federal prison. Mark Colville is an American social justice and Catholic Worker activist. He is the founder of the Amistad Catholic Worker community in New Haven, Connecticut, which works on issues including homelessness, housing justice, and anti-war organizing.

Colville has been involved in anti-military activism for years, including protests outside U.S. drone bases. In April 2018, he was one of the seven members of the Kings Bay Plowshares 7 who entered the Kings Bay Naval Submarine Base to symbolically protest nuclear weapons. For this action he was convicted on federal charges alongside his co-defendants, and he chose not to seek bail on conscience grounds.

Colville has also been recognised locally for his activism and community work, including as a New Haven Register “Persons of the Year.” The Prince of Peace Plowshares was a six-person nonviolent direct-disarmament action at Bath Iron Works in Bath, Maine on February 14, 1997. Philip Berrigan, Susan Crane, Stephen Kelly S.J., Mark Colville, Steve Baggarly, and Tom Lewis-Borbely entered the shipyard and hammered on, and poured blood on, the Tomahawk cruise-missile vertical launching system installed on the destroyer USS The Sullivans (DDG-68) under construction. They were charged in U.S. District Court for the District of Maine with conspiracy and damage to government property, with prosecutors alleging $28,000 in damage. All six were convicted; in addition to prison, each received two years of supervised release and a $4,000 restitution fine.

He pleaded guilty to attempting to destroy an electrical transmission line used in interstate commerce. He was sentenced to 6 years in federal prison and ordered to pay $19,821 in restitution — the longest sentence of the Arizona Five. The Earth First! prosecutions are widely cited as the first U.S. Green Scare case.

description:
Irish national from Dundalk along the militarized border separating Northern Ireland from the rest of the country. He had been in the United States only a few months at the time of his arrest. Judge A. David Mazzone refused to allow him to remain free pending appeal, calling him 'a danger to the community,' and doubled his sentence from four to eight years. The FBI watched Quigley for 16 hours a day for ten weeks (30 agents) and photographed him with his girlfriend sunbathing on a beach. Held at Connecticut federal facility.

Martin P. Quigley was one of the defendants in a high-profile Boston federal case involving Irish republican-linked weapons technology. Prosecutors alleged that the effort was aimed at providing the IRA with the means to counter British Army helicopters, focusing on specialized components and technical know-how rather than conventional gun-running alone.

Quigley was arrested in the late 1980s and convicted in federal court in Boston on charges tied to the conspiracy and unlawful export-related conduct. He served a federal prison term in the United States and, after completing his sentence, was released and deported to Ireland in the mid-1990s.

A former engineer and Peace Corps volunteer, he turned to organizing after the Kent State killings and moved to Baltimore in 1983 to work for Nuclear Free America, later joining the American Friends Service Committee, Maryland Peace Action and the Baltimore Nonviolence Center. He took part in five Plowshares-related disarmament actions, four of them alongside Philip Berrigan. Most of his arrests ended in citations, dismissals, probation or suspended sentences; his clearest jail terms were 30 days in 1995 and 10 days in 1999, both for actions at the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory. In 2005-2006 an undercover Maryland State Police officer infiltrated his groups and logged him in a regional intelligence database under classifications including "Terrorism-Anti-War Protestors," making him a prominent example of post-September 11 surveillance treating nonviolent dissent as terrorism.

description:
Michele Naar-Obed is associated with Catholic pacifist direct action against nuclear weapons and militarism, particularly actions that target the infrastructure of submarine- and missile-based deterrence. In August 1995, she was among activists who entered Newport News Shipbuilding and boarded the USS Greenville while it was in dry dock, pouring blood and hammering on areas associated with cruise-missile capability as a symbolic attempt to “disarm” the weapon system. She was arrested and prosecuted following the action.

Her subsequent activism is also described as involving repeated civil-disobedience arrests and post-release supervision constraints that treated peace-community ties as suspect. Across these episodes, Naar-Obed’s public profile is rooted in a pattern of nonviolent but illegal-entry protests paired with willingness to accept incarceration as part of antiwar witness. On August 6, 1995 (Hiroshima Day) Michele Naar-Obed and Brennan Plowshares partners boarded a U.S. Navy fast-attack submarine in port and used hammers and blood to symbolically disarm it as part of the "Jubilee Plowshares/East" action. She received 12 months in federal prison. Her probation was later revoked and she was returned to federal custody in July 1999.

While Susan Frankel and Bill Streit hammered and poured blood on a KC-135 refueling plane and a cruise-missile-armed B-52 bomber, Cole and Ciaron O'Reilly entered from the opposite end of the runway, marked it with a cross of blood, spray-painted messages including "Love Your Enemies — Jesus Christ" and "Isaiah Strikes Again," and hammered on the runway for about an hour before being detained. The four were indicted on January 9, 1991 on federal charges of conspiracy and destruction of government property, facing up to 15 years. After about two months in jail they were released pre-trial on March 6, 1991, then convicted by a jury in Syracuse in May 1991 and on August 20, 1991 sentenced to twelve months in prison and $1,800 in restitution. Released from federal prison on June 15, 1992 after serving about ten months, she was then held for immigration proceedings and freed on bail pending a deportation hearing, returning to New Zealand under a court-ordered voluntary deportation in October 1992. She later completed a master's degree in law and works as a barrister providing legal aid in Christchurch.

name: Nasser Ahmed
description:
Nasser Ahmed became a prominent figure in late-1990s civil-liberties disputes over the use of “secret evidence” in immigration detention. An Egyptian immigrant living in Brooklyn, he became linked—through community and legal work—to the orbit of the high-profile prosecution of Omar Abdel-Rahman, and U.S. immigration authorities treated him as a national security concern.

He was detained in 1996 and spent years in solitary confinement while the government relied on classified allegations that he and his lawyers could not fully review or rebut. The case drew sustained organizing and legal challenges, and immigration adjudicators later concluded that, once a declassified version of the allegations was available for meaningful rebuttal, key claims did not hold up. He was ultimately released, and his detention became a central example cited by critics of secret-evidence procedures.

name: Oliver Sachio Coe
description:
Oliver Sachio Coe participated in the same August 1998 Colorado missile-site action as Daniel Sicken, joining an anti-nuclear protest that intentionally crossed into restricted space to make a public moral claim against nuclear deterrence and first-strike weapons systems. The action relied on symbolic property damage and ritualized “witness” practices common in certain faith-based resistance traditions, and it culminated in arrest at the scene.

Like Sicken, Coe was prosecuted federally under statutes treating the breach and damage as conspiratorial sabotage rather than civil disobedience. He was convicted and sentenced to federal prison (receiving a shorter term than Sicken in reported sentencing summaries), and the case remains an example of how anti-nuclear activists have been charged and imprisoned for actions framed as nonviolent but carried out at highly secured defense sites. Sachio Oliver Coe was one of two members of the Minuteman III Plowshares affinity group that entered Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missile silo N-8 near Greeley, Colorado on August 6, 1998 — the 53rd anniversary of the U.S. atomic bombing of Hiroshima — and hammered on the silo cover and equipment. He was found guilty of conspiracy to destroy national defense property, sabotage, and destruction of government property. After he and Sicken told the judge they would not promise to return for January 1999 sentencing, their bond was revoked and they were taken into custody.

On August 6, 1998 — the 53rd anniversary of the U.S. atomic bombing of Hiroshima — Daniel Sicken and Sachio Oliver Coe entered Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missile silo N-8 near Greeley, Colorado, and hammered on the silo cover and equipment. The action took the name Minuteman III Plowshares.

Ramón Labañino Salazar is part of the Cuban Five serving 30 years, reduced from a life sentence plus 18 years.

The cell gathered intelligence on right-wing Cuban-American exile organizations — Alpha 66, Brothers to the Rescue, Omega 7 — that the Cuban government accused of armed attacks on Cuban tourist infrastructure. Arrested in Miami on September 12, 1998. Tried in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida and convicted in June 2001 of conspiracy to commit espionage and acting as an unregistered foreign agent. Originally sentenced to life plus 18 years; later resentenced on remand to 30 years. Held at USP Beaumont. He was released on December 17, 2014 in the U.S.-Cuba prisoner swap brokered by President Barack Obama and Pope Francis, and returned to Havana as a national hero.

description: James Richard Scarce, known as Rik Scarce, is a sociologist and author who was jailed for civil contempt in 1993 after refusing, on scholarly-privilege grounds, to tell a federal grand jury about confidential conversations with a research subject. As a doctoral student at Washington State University, Scarce had interviewed radical environmental and animal-liberation activists for his book Eco-Warriors. After a 1991 Animal Liberation Front raid caused roughly 100,000 dollars in damage to university animal-research laboratories — an action linked to Rod Coronado, who had stayed at the Scarce family home — a grand jury in Spokane, Washington demanded that Scarce reveal what his sources had told him. name: Roy Bourgeois
description:
A Maryknoll priest and Vietnam veteran, Bourgeois became a leading critic of U.S. military policy in Latin America and founded School of the Americas Watch. His activism relied heavily on repeated nonviolent civil disobedience aimed at military institutions—especially protests connected to Fort Benning, where the U.S. Army’s School of the Americas operated.

Those protests led to multiple arrests and prison terms. In 1983, he was convicted on trespassing and impersonation charges linked to an anti‑SOA action and served 18 months in federal prison; he was arrested again in subsequent protests as well. Earlier, he had also been arrested and deported from Bolivia in 1975 after organizing alongside campesino and labor movements.

A former Catholic priest and longtime human-rights campaigner, Bourgeois is best known for founding School of the Americas Watch and building a sustained movement to close School of the Americas at Fort Benning. His activism has centered on U.S. policy in Latin America and the consequences of military training and counterinsurgency doctrine for civilians; he became a prominent organizer of large annual demonstrations as well as smaller acts of civil disobedience that repeatedly led to arrest on trespass or unlawful-entry charges.

His history of arrest connected to political activism predates that campaign. While working with poor communities in Bolivia, he was arrested during the dictatorship of Hugo Banzer and later deported; he also faced arrest in the United States in connection with actions aimed at highlighting violence and repression linked to conflicts in places such as El Salvador.

She also pleaded guilty in 2003 to second-degree murder for the April 21, 1975 SLA bank robbery in Carmichael, California in which a customer named Myrna Opsahl was killed; she was sentenced to an additional 6 years to run concurrently. description:
Father Steve Kelly SJ is an American Jesuit priest and one of the most prolific Plowshares activists in U.S. history. He was a member of the Prince of Peace Plowshares affinity group that boarded the USS The Sullivans at the Bath Iron Works in Maine on February 12, 1997 and hammered on the Tomahawk cruise missile launching system. Kelly was sentenced to ~28 months in federal prison and served at LSCI Allenwood, Pennsylvania, released in June 1999. He has participated in additional Plowshares actions including the November 2, 2009 Disarm Now Plowshares at Naval Base Kitsap-Bangor and the April 4, 2018 Kings Bay Plowshares 7 action at the Trident submarine base in Georgia.

On February 12, 1997, four Plowshares activists — Susan Crane, Steve Kelly SJ, Tom Lewis, and Steve Baggarly — boarded the USS The Sullivans, a guided-missile destroyer being outfitted with the Tomahawk cruise launching system at the Bath Iron Works shipyard in Maine, and hammered on and poured blood over the missile launchers. The action took the name Prince of Peace Plowshares. Steve (Stephen) Kelly, S.J. is an American Jesuit priest and peace activist associated with the Plowshares movement. He has spent much of the past decade in prison for participating in nonviolent actions against U.S. nuclear weapons, including protests that involved hammering on D-5 Trident missile components.

Kelly was one of the seven members of the Kings Bay Plowshares 7, who on April 4, 2018 entered the Kings Bay Naval Submarine Base in Georgia as a symbolic act of disarmament against nuclear weapons. A federal court convicted the group on felony and misdemeanor charges. For his role, Kelly was sentenced in 2020 to 33 months’ imprisonment plus probation and restitution, with credit for time already served awaiting trial. Stephen Michael Kelly, age 69, was one of the Kings Bay Plowshares 7 (KBP7) Catholic anti-nuclear activists who broke into Kings Bay Naval Submarine Base in St. Marys GA on April 4-5, 2018 to protest Trident-class nuclear weapons. Convicted on all four counts; 33 months federal prison.

name: Sundiata Jawanza
description:
Sundiata Jawanza, born Darvin Allen, has been imprisoned in the South Carolina state prison system since 1995, serving a life sentence for murder and accessory after the fact of armed robbery. He has expressed remorse for the offenses of his youth and during his three decades inside has become one of the most consequential prison-rights organizers in the United States.

He is a founder of Jailhouse Lawyers Speak, the prisoner-led network that since 2018 has organized national prison work strikes and the Free Alabama Movement-style campaigns against forced prison labor. He is Co-Chair of the National Lawyers Guild Mass Incarceration Committee and the Mass Defense Committee, and the Jailhouse Lawyer Vice President on the NLGs National Executive Committee. He is also an Imam who serves as the spiritual guide for the Muslim population in his facility, and a certified peer support specialist who teaches substance-use and mental-health classes inside.

South Carolina prison authorities have responded to his organizing by holding him in closed custody. In April 2023 he was transferred to the Turbeville Correctional Institution to complete the Addiction Treatment Unit program in support of his parole eligibility. The Jericho Movement classifies him as a politicized prisoner — a person originally incarcerated for ordinary criminal charges who has become a political prisoner through subsequent organizing inside.

name: Susan Crane
description:
Susan Crane is widely described as a long-running anti-nuclear resister whose activism has relied on civil disobedience at military and weapons-related facilities. A major episode in her arrest history centers on the 2009 “Disarm Now” action at Naval Base Kitsap-Bangor, where a small group cut fences, walked deep into the base toward a nuclear weapons storage area, performed prayers and symbolic gestures, and were arrested by military security.

The case led to felony convictions (including conspiracy, trespass, and property-damage counts) and a 15-month federal prison sentence imposed in 2011. Crane’s record is often discussed as part of a decades-long pattern of arrests for entering restricted spaces to challenge nuclear policy, with the Kitsap-Bangor prosecution serving as one of the clearest examples of the legal consequences imposed on Plowshares-style actions. Imprisoned February 2, 2001 for probation violation tied to the 'Plowshares vs Depleted Uranium' direct-disarmament action of December 19, 1999, in which Catholic Worker / Plowshares activists hammered on A-10 anti-tank warplanes (which fire depleted-uranium rounds) at the Maryland Air National Guard's Warfield ANG Base. The probation itself stemmed from the Prince of Peace Plowshares action of February 14, 1997, when six activists hammered and poured blood on a Tomahawk cruise-missile launching system aboard the USS The Sullivans at Bath Iron Works in Maine.

name: Susan Rosenberg
description:
Susan Rosenberg was a New York-born radical who joined the May 19th Communist Organization in the late 1970s and went underground after being implicated as an accessory in the 1979 prison escape of Assata Shakur and the 1981 Brink's robbery. On November 29, 1984 she and Tim Blunk were arrested in Cherry Hill, New Jersey while unloading 740 pounds of dynamite, weapons, and false-identity documents at a storage locker. Sentenced to 58 years for weapons and explosives possession — an unprecedented sentence widely condemned by legal observers — she pled guilty in 1990 to conspiracy in the Resistance Conspiracy Case with no additional time. President Clinton commuted her sentence on January 20, 2001 and she was released after 16 years; she has since worked in HIV/AIDS advocacy and prisoner rights. Rosenberg became involved in radical left politics in the late 1970s and 1980s, aligning herself with anti-imperialist causes and prisoner advocacy. She was associated with networks connected to the May 19 Communist Organization and was sought by the Federal Bureau of Investigation during a period when underground groups carried out bombings and robberies framed as political action. She also had associations with the Weather Underground milieu.

In 1984 she was arrested in New Jersey after authorities discovered a large cache of weapons, explosives, and false identification. She was convicted on weapons/explosives-related charges and sentenced to 58 years in federal prison; in 2001, Bill Clinton commuted her sentence to time served. After release, she remained active in social-justice work and continued advocacy related to incarceration and political repression.

name: Wen Ho Lee
description:
Wen Ho Lee is a Taiwanese-American nuclear scientist who worked at Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico for two decades and became the central figure in one of the most discredited espionage prosecutions in U.S. history. In December 1999, after a year of leaks portraying him as a Chinese spy who had stolen the United States most sensitive nuclear weapons design data, he was indicted on 59 felony counts. He was held in solitary confinement at the Santa Fe County Detention Center for nine months — most of it shackled when out of his cell, including for family visits — without bond and without ever being charged with espionage.

The governments case collapsed in the summer of 2000. On September 13, 2000, Lee pleaded guilty to a single felony count of mishandling classified information and was released for time served. The other 58 counts were dropped. Federal District Judge James A. Parker took the extraordinary step of issuing an apology from the bench, telling Lee that the government had embarrassed our entire nation and led me into ordering your detention last December. Lee later won a $1.65 million settlement from the federal government and several news organizations whose reporting had been driven by anonymous leaks from prosecutors.
